questions.q: You add a 50-day moving average to your chart. What is that line actually showing you?
choices: The average close over recent days
Today's high, low and closing price
Where price will most likely go next
The stock's fair value per share
questions.answer: The average close over recent days
questions.why: The average close over recent days, here the last 50. Each day the newest close gets added and the oldest drops off, so the line moves along with price. It shows you the direction. It doesn't predict anything. And it lags, because it's built from past prices. We use the 50 and 200-day simple averages with the 9 and 20 EMA. A healthy stock holds above its rising averages.
questions.lesson_line: A moving average smooths the noise and shows direction. It never predicts.

wrong.Today's high, low and closing price: That's one day's bar. A moving average averages many days.
wrong.Where price will most likely go next: It doesn't predict. It shows the current direction, and it lags.
wrong.The stock's fair value per share: It's only an average of past prices. It says nothing about what the company is worth.

questions.simple: The average closing price over the last 50 days, updated each day as a new close comes in.

deeper.example: ChartSchool says a moving average defines the current direction but does not predict it, and lags because it's based on past prices. Schwab notes the oldest day is subtracted and the current day added each day.

questions.q: Five closes in a row: $20, $22, $24, $25 and $23. What's the 5-day simple moving average?
questions.why: $22.80. Add the five closes, then divide by five. $20 + $22 + $24 + $25 + $23 is $114. $114 divided by 5 is $22.80. That's all a simple average is. Your chart does this every day for you, dropping the oldest close and adding the newest. Doing it once by hand shows you why the line lags: an old close counts just as much as today's.
questions.lesson_line: A simple moving average adds up the closes and divides by how many there are.
questions.simple: It's $22.80. You add the five closes and divide by five.

wrong.$114.00: You added the five closes and never divided.
wrong.$28.50: You divided the $114 sum by 4 instead of 5.
wrong.$21.50: You averaged only the oldest and newest closes, $20 and $23.

deeper.example: ChartSchool's example: a 5-day simple moving average is the five-day sum of closing prices divided by five. Fidelity calls the SMA simply the average price over the period.

questions.q: On your chart, the 20 EMA turns before the 20-day simple average does. What makes the EMA quicker?
questions.why: It weights recent prices more. A simple average counts every day in its window the same. The EMA leans on the latest closes, so it reacts faster and turns first. That's why we use the 9 and 20 EMA as our shorter lines. They stay close to a stock that's moving. It's still built from past prices, so it can't see ahead. It's just less late.
questions.lesson_line: The EMA reacts faster, the simple average is steadier. Neither one sees the future.

wrong.Weights every day the same: That's the simple average, and it's the slower one.
wrong.Uses only the daily highs: EMAs are built from closing prices, like most moving averages.
wrong.Looks ahead of price: No average looks ahead. Every one is built from past prices.

questions.simple: The EMA gives more weight to recent prices, so it reacts faster than a simple average of the same length.

deeper.example: ChartSchool says exponential averages turn before simple ones. Fidelity says the EMA has a shorter delay than an SMA of the same period.

questions.q: When a stock turns, its 200-day moving average turns faster than its 20-day.
questions.why: False. It's the other way around. The 200-day holds 200 days of prices, so a few new days barely move it. The 20-day only holds 20, so it turns quickly. Short averages react fast. Long ones are smooth but slow. That's why I use the 200-day for the big trend and the shorter lines for what's happening right now.
questions.lesson_line: Short averages turn fast. The 200-day holds so much history that it turns slowly.
questions.simple: False. A longer average holds more past prices, so it lags more and turns more slowly.

deeper.example: Investopedia says a 200-day average has a much greater degree of lag than a 20-day one. ChartSchool compares short averages to speedboats, nimble and quick to change.

questions.q: The 50-day on your chart just crossed up through the 200-day. What's that called?
questions.why: A golden cross. That's a shorter average crossing up through a longer one, and the classic version is the 50-day over the 200-day. The reverse, the 50-day dropping under the 200-day, is a death cross. It's two averages crossing, not price breaking a level. For a long I want the 50-day over the 200-day. That's mostly a must, not always. But the cross itself comes late, because both lines lag, so price will have told you first.
questions.lesson_line: The 50-day over the 200-day is a golden cross. Mostly a must for a long, but the cross comes late.

wrong.Death cross: That's the opposite, the 50-day crossing below the 200-day.
wrong.Breakout: A breakout is price clearing a level. Here two averages crossed each other.
wrong.Bearish divergence: Divergence is price against an indicator like RSI. Two averages crossing is a golden or death cross.

questions.simple: A golden cross. The shorter 50-day average crossed up through the longer 200-day.

deeper.example: ChartSchool associates the golden cross with the 50-day crossing above the 200-day, and Fidelity calls it a bullish signal. ChartSchool also notes crossovers produce relatively late signals, since both averages lag.

questions.q: A death cross is an early warning. It shows up before a stock starts to fall.
questions.why: False. It comes late. For the 50-day to drop under the 200-day, the stock has been sliding for a while. Both averages lag, so the cross confirms weakness that price already showed you with lower highs and lower lows. Read price first. And once a stock is under the 200-day, we don't buy it anyway. That's a hard no for stocks.
questions.lesson_line: By the time the 50-day crosses under the 200-day, price already told you. Read price first.
questions.simple: False. Both averages lag, so the cross shows up after the price has already been falling.

deeper.trap: The trap is waiting for the cross before you act. ChartSchool says crossovers give relatively late signals because both averages lag. Investopedia calls the death cross a coincident indicator of market weakness rather than a leading one.

reasons: fixed before (f93 removed; Investopedia read from the Internet Archive)

questions.story: A stock is in an uptrend and pulls back to its rising 50-day average. It dips about 1% under the line during the day, then closes back above it.
questions.q: What do you make of the dip under the line?
questions.why: Normal. Moving averages aren't exact lines. Price overshoots them all the time, especially the longer ones. Here it poked about 1% under the rising 50-day and closed back above it. That's a stock holding its average, not losing it. One intraday poke doesn't end an uptrend. That takes a lower low under the last dip. A pullback to a rising 50-day that holds is a spot where good stocks often get bought.
questions.lesson_line: Treat a moving average as a zone. One intraday poke through it isn't a broken trend.

wrong.The uptrend has now ended: One dip under a line doesn't end an uptrend. A lower low under the last dip does.
wrong.A death cross has formed: A death cross is the 50-day crossing below the 200-day. Here price dipped under one line. No averages crossed.
wrong.The 50-day is broken for good: It closed back above. Averages work as zones, and price overshoots them.

questions.simple: Normal. A moving average works as a zone, and the stock closed back above it.

deeper.counter: The read changes only if the trend itself breaks. ChartSchool warns not to expect exact support from moving averages, because markets overshoot. Its Dow Theory keeps an uptrend in place until a lower low forms under the previous low. Watch that low, not the line.

questions.q: Someone in chat says the stock you want is way too extended. What does that mean?
choices: Down a lot from its 52-week high
Stuck in a tight sideways range
questions.why: Stretched far above its averages. We read every chart in percents, and one of them is how far a stock sits above its moving averages. Extended doesn't mean it has to fall. It means the move already started without you. Buy it now and your stop is a long way down, or you're buying right before a pullback. If it's more than 10% above its 9 EMA, we skip it.
questions.lesson_line: Extended is a measurement, not a feeling. Know the percent before you chase.

wrong.Down a lot from its 52-week high: That's the other number we track, percent off the highs. Extended is the stretch above the averages.
wrong.Stuck in a tight sideways range: That's a stock resting. Extended is a stock that has run far from its averages.
wrong.Trading after the market's close: That's a time of day, not a chart read. On a chart, extended means stretched above the averages.

questions.simple: The price has run far above its moving averages, and we measure that stretch in percent.

deeper.example: ChartSchool's Distance From Moving Average indicator measures the same stretch. Its glossary calls a stock that has risen past its pivot point a risky buy, because it has already begun its advance.

questions.q: Your stock closes at $66 and its 50-day sits at $60. How far above the 50-day is it?
questions.why: 10%. Take the gap, then divide by the average. $66 minus $60 is $6. $6 divided by $60 is 10%. Always divide by the average, not the close. Percent is what lets you compare: a $5 gap on a $20 stock means far more than on a $500 stock. Just know which line you measured from. Our too-stretched line uses the 9 EMA, not the 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Measure extension in percent, not dollars. Then any two stocks compare fairly.
questions.simple: It's 10% above. The gap between the close and the average is one tenth of the $60 average.

deeper.counter: Always say which average you measured from. Our skip line uses the 9 EMA: we skip a long that is more than 10% above its 9 EMA. This question measures from the 50-day, so its 10% is not the same test. ChartSchool measures distance from a moving average as a percent of the average.

reasons: house rule (h1, owner's rulebook A14 and C29)

wrong.9.1%: You divided the $6 gap by the $66 close, not the $60 average.
wrong.6.0%: You took the $6 gap as a percent and never divided by $60.
wrong.110.0%: That's the close as a percent of the average, not the gap.

questions.story: A leader broke out three weeks ago. It now sits 25% above its 50-day average, its widest stretch in a year. You missed the entry.
questions.q: What's the play now?
choices: Wait for a pullback or a new setup
Buy now before it runs further
Short it, it has to drop back
Buy half now and half on a dip
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback or a new setup
questions.why: Wait for a pullback or a new setup. At 25% over the 50-day, the move happened without you. Buy here and your stop is a long way down. Put it tight instead and the first normal pullback takes you out. I'd rather miss it than chase it. Leaders give you another spot. Let it rest and pull back toward its rising averages, or build a new base. Then buy that with a stop that makes sense.
questions.lesson_line: I'd rather miss it than chase it. Leaders give you another spot.

wrong.Buy now before it runs further: That's chasing. The move already started, so your risk to a sensible stop is huge.
wrong.Buy half now and half on a dip: We don't scale in. We buy the full size at one price with one stop. Adding on a dip is never the plan.
wrong.Short it, it has to drop back: Stretched isn't the same as done. Far above the average can just be strength in a strong uptrend.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback or a new setup. Buying this stretched means buying after the move already ran.

deeper.trap: The trap is fear of missing out. ChartSchool calls a stock past its buy point a risky buy, because the advance has already begun. After a big advance, it adds, waiting for a pullback may be prudent.

reasons: touches our no-chasing rules (rulebook C28, C29); the key agrees with them

questions.q: RSI on your stock reads 76. Which RSI reading do traders call overbought?
questions.why: Above 70. RSI runs from zero to 100. Above 70 is the classic overbought line and below 30 the classic oversold line, so 76 counts. 50 is just the middle of the scale. And 14 is the lookback setting, how many bars RSI uses, not a level. Know the lines, but don't trade off them alone. A strong stock can sit above 70 for a long time.
questions.lesson_line: On RSI, 70 is the classic overbought line and 30 the oversold line. Neither one is a trade.

wrong.RSI below 30: That's oversold, the other end of the scale.
wrong.RSI above 50: 50 is the middle of the scale, not an extreme.
wrong.RSI above 14: 14 is the lookback, how many periods RSI uses. It's a setting, not a level.

questions.simple: Above 70 is overbought on the RSI scale, and below 30 is oversold.

deeper.example: Wilder considered RSI overbought above 70 and oversold below 30. ChartSchool, Investopedia and Fidelity give the same traditional levels. Investopedia words it as 70 or above.

questions.q: Your stock's RSI just pushed over 70. That means it's about to fall.
questions.why: False. Overbought just means the stock has run far and fast. In a strong uptrend RSI can sit up there for a long time while price keeps climbing. It works better in a choppy range than in a trend. Overbought isn't bearish. At most it says a pullback might be due. I'd never sell a leader on an RSI number alone. Price breaking its trend is what gets me out.
questions.lesson_line: Overbought can stay overbought. I don't sell a leader on RSI alone.
questions.simple: False. In a strong uptrend, RSI can stay overbought for a long time while price keeps rising.

deeper.trap: The trap is selling a leader because RSI says overbought. ChartSchool says overbought is not the same as bearish. Investopedia notes RSI works best in trading ranges, and Fidelity says RSI can stay overbought for extended periods during strong trends.

questions.story: A stock has been in a steady downtrend for months. Its RSI drops to 25. A friend says it's oversold, so it has to bounce.
questions.q: What's the better read?
choices: It can stay oversold for a long time
Oversold means it is time to buy now
RSI 25 means the downtrend has ended
It should bounce once RSI nears 20
questions.answer: It can stay oversold for a long time
questions.why: It can stay oversold for a long time. RSI at 25 is under the classic 30 line, sure. But in a steady downtrend that reading can hang down there while price keeps falling. Oversold is an alert, not a buy signal. Falling stocks look cheap all the way down. Price has to turn first, a higher low and then a higher high. And a stock that's fallen for months is probably under its 200-day, where we don't buy stocks at all. I'd rather buy strength than guess a bottom.
questions.lesson_line: Oversold is an alert, not a buy signal. I'd rather buy strength than guess a bottom.

wrong.Oversold means it is time to buy now: That's the mistake. Oversold is an alert, not a buy signal.
wrong.RSI 25 means the downtrend has ended: A reading doesn't end a trend. Price ends it, with a higher low and then a higher high.
wrong.It should bounce once RSI nears 20: No reading promises a bounce. A rally may not come soon, or at all.

questions.simple: It can stay oversold for a long time. A weak stock can keep falling while its RSI stays low.

deeper.trap: Investopedia warns that stocks that keep falling look cheap all the way down, and that many traders wait for the price to start moving up before buying. In a strong downtrend, Fidelity's slides note, an oscillator can stay in its oversold zone and give many false signals.

questions.q: You've got RSI plotted under your chart. What is it actually measuring?
choices: A stock's recent gains vs losses
A stock's move vs the S&P 500
questions.answer: A stock's recent gains vs losses
questions.why: A stock's recent gains against its recent losses. RSI looks at one stock alone. It weighs the size of its up moves against its down moves. The standard setting is 14 periods, on a 0 to 100 scale. It doesn't compare the stock to the market. That's relative strength, a different thing with a confusingly similar name. Know which one you're looking at.
questions.lesson_line: RSI weighs a stock's own recent gains against its own recent losses. It never looks at the market.

wrong.A stock's move vs the S&P 500: RSI looks at one stock alone. Comparing to the index is relative strength.
wrong.Today's volume vs average volume: That's relative volume. RSI only uses price changes.
wrong.Price vs its 200-day average: That's distance from an average. RSI uses the size of the up moves and down moves.

questions.simple: RSI measures a stock's own recent gains against its own recent losses.

deeper.example: ChartSchool builds RSI from RS, average gain and average loss, over 14 periods by Wilder's default. Fidelity says RSI compares recent gains to recent losses. Investopedia says it compares strength on up days with strength on down days.

questions.q: You're picking between two names for your watchlist, and a friend says check the RS. What does relative strength compare?
choices: A stock's move vs a benchmark
Its price today vs a year ago
questions.answer: A stock's move vs a benchmark
questions.why: A stock's move against a benchmark, like the market. If the index is up a little and your stock is up a lot, that's relative strength. It's a ratio of one against the other. When that line rises, your stock is beating the index. It has nothing to do with RSI. I want stocks beating the market, not just rising with it. Those are the ones that lead.
questions.lesson_line: I want stocks beating the market, not just rising with it.

wrong.Today's volume vs normal volume: That's relative volume, a different read.
wrong.Price vs its moving average: That's distance from an average. Relative strength compares the stock with the market.
wrong.Its price today vs a year ago: That's the stock against its own past. Relative strength compares it with an index.

questions.simple: It compares a stock's move with a benchmark, like a market index, to see if it beats the market.

deeper.example: ChartSchool's price relative is a ratio chart comparing one security with another. Fidelity says it's often used against a market index. The CMT Association notes it has nothing to do with Wilder's RSI.

questions.q: Someone calls a stock a leader. On a chart, what makes it one?
choices: The biggest company in its industry
The stock with the highest share price
questions.why: It's beating the market. On a chart, leadership is about performance, not fame or size. The biggest company in an industry can lag. A stock with a high share price can lag. Check it against the index and against its group. If it's beating both, it's leading. Those are the names we want on our list.
questions.lesson_line: Leaders are found by performance, not fame. Check the stock against the index and its group.

wrong.The biggest company in its industry: That's the business meaning, market share. On a chart, a leader is the stock beating the market.
wrong.The most heavily traded stock: Volume shows activity, not leadership. A busy stock can still lag.
wrong.The stock with the highest share price: A share price says nothing about performance. A leader is judged by its returns against the market.

questions.simple: A leader is a stock doing better than the market, judged by how it moves, not by its size.

deeper.trap: The trap is the business meaning. Investopedia's market leader is the company with the largest market share. On a chart, ChartSchool's leader is an industry or company outperforming the market.

questions.story: Over one month, the S&P 500 falls 8%. KZRN falls 2%. BLTQ falls 15%.
questions.q: Which one showed relative strength?
choices: KZRN, it fell less than the index
Neither, you'd need each RSI first
questions.answer: KZRN, it fell less than the index
questions.why: KZRN. Relative strength is about the gap to the index, not the direction. The market fell 8% and KZRN only fell 2%, so it held up far better. BLTQ fell 15%, way worse than the index. That's relative weakness. Watch the names that hold up while the market drops. When the market turns, those are often the next leaders. That's where I start building my list.
questions.lesson_line: Watch who holds up when the market drops. That's where the next leaders hide.

wrong.BLTQ, it fell the most: Falling more than the index is relative weakness, the opposite.
wrong.Neither, both went down: Relative strength is about the gap to the index, not the direction. KZRN fell far less than the market.
wrong.Neither, you'd need each RSI first: Relative strength isn't RSI. RSI rates one stock alone. Relative strength compares the stock with the index.

questions.simple: KZRN. It fell less than the index, and holding up better than the market is relative strength.

deeper.example: A falling stock can show relative strength. ChartSchool's price relative rises when a stock advances more than the S&P 500 or declines less. It adds that stocks holding up best during a decline are often the leaders when the market turns around.

questions.q: Your stock prints a new high, but RSI tops out lower than it did at the last high. What's that called?
questions.why: Bearish divergence. Price made a higher high, but the momentum behind it made a lower high. The move is running on less fuel. That's a warning, not a sell signal. I want price itself to crack before I act, like losing a key level or making a lower low. Until then, it's a note on the chart.
questions.lesson_line: Divergence is a yellow light. Wait for price to confirm before you act on it.

wrong.Bullish divergence: That's the mirror: a lower low in price with a higher low in the indicator.
wrong.Golden cross: That's two moving averages crossing, not price against an indicator.
wrong.Trend confirmation: Confirmation would be RSI making a higher high too. Here it didn't.

questions.simple: Bearish divergence. Price rose to a new high while the momentum behind it made a lower high.

deeper.example: ChartSchool defines it as price recording a higher high while the indicator forms a lower high, and Investopedia calls it negative divergence. Fidelity says a new high that RSI does not confirm can signal a reversal. ChartSchool says to confirm RSI signals with other tools.

questions.q: In a strong uptrend, bearish RSI divergences give a lot of false signals.
questions.why: True. A strong uptrend can show divergence after divergence before it ever tops. Each one looks like the end, and most aren't. RSI just can't keep up with a stock that keeps running. So in a leader, a divergence is a note on the chart, not an exit. Let price break first. Your trail under the rising averages will get you out when it's really over.
questions.lesson_line: One divergence in a strong leader is a note, not an exit. Let price break first.
questions.simple: True. A strong uptrend can show many bearish divergences while the stock keeps going up.

deeper.trap: The trap is selling a strong leader on the first bearish divergence. ChartSchool says a strong uptrend can show numerous bearish divergences before a top materializes. Fidelity's slides add that in strong trends an oscillator gives many false signals on corrections.

reasons: statement reworded by the final checker: the 'does not prove' wording was a negated-absolute tell

questions.q: Your stock trades 3,000,000 shares today against a 50-day average of 1,200,000. What's its relative volume?
questions.why: 2.5x. Divide today's volume by the average. 3,000,000 divided by 1,200,000 is 2.5, so today is two and a half times a normal day. A reading of 1.0 would be a normal day. On a breakout, that's the kind of number that tells you people showed up. It raises the grade.
questions.lesson_line: Relative volume is today against normal. 1.0 is a normal day, and 2.5 means people showed up.
questions.simple: It's 2.5x. Today's 3,000,000 shares divided by the 1,200,000 average is two and a half times normal.

wrong.0.4x: You flipped it and divided the average by today's volume.
wrong.25.0x: Decimal slip. You moved the point one place too far.
wrong.1.5x: You used the extra volume over the average, not today's volume itself.

deeper.example: ChartSchool: an RVOL of 2.5 means the current bar's volume is 2.5 times the normal volume, and a value of 1.0 means it matches the average.

questions.q: The volume bar under today's candle towers over the rest. What does heavy volume tell you?
choices: Far more shares traded than usual
The price moved a lot that day
It was the most traded stock that day
questions.answer: Far more shares traded than usual
questions.why: Far more shares traded than usual. Heavy is measured against the stock's own average, not against other stocks. It doesn't mean buyers beat sellers, because every share bought is a share sold. It isn't the size of the price move either. A stock can trade huge volume and barely move. What heavy volume tells you is that a lot of people cared about that day. Then you read the candle to see who won.
questions.lesson_line: Volume is the crowd. Heavy volume means a lot of people cared, and the candle shows who won.

wrong.The price moved a lot that day: Price and volume are separate reads. A big move can come on light volume.
wrong.Buyers outnumbered sellers that day: Every share bought is a share sold. Heavy volume means more shares changed hands, not more buyers.
wrong.It was the most traded stock that day: Heavy is judged against the stock's own average, not against other stocks.

questions.simple: Far more shares than usual changed hands that day, compared with the stock's own average.

deeper.example: ChartSchool: for every buyer there is a seller, 100 shares bought = 100 shares sold. Schwab notes volume can rise with no rise in price.

questions.story: A stock in a strong uptrend dips 6% over four days. Volume on the dip runs well below its 50-day average.
questions.q: What's the light volume telling you?
choices: Volume doesn't matter on a dip
questions.why: Likely just a pullback. The stock dipped 6% in four days, and volume dried up the whole way down. Nobody's rushing for the exits. That's what a normal pullback in a strong stock looks like. If volume had spiked on the drop, I'd worry about real selling. Likely isn't certain, so keep your stop where it is and let the stock show you.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet dips in a strong trend are normal. Loud dips get my attention.

wrong.Big sellers are taking over: Big sellers leave heavy volume behind. This dip is quiet.
wrong.Volume doesn't matter on a dip: It does. A quiet dip and a loud dip read very differently.
wrong.Likely weak demand ahead: Light volume on the way down means sellers aren't pressing. Concern looks limited, not growing.

questions.simple: Likely just a pullback. Volume dried up on the dip, so few people are rushing to sell.

deeper.example: ChartSchool says a pullback with low relative volume is likely just a pullback, while heavier volume on the drop shows traders committed to the move down. Schwab adds that a decline without above average volume implies investor concern is limited.

questions.q: After a long run-up, your stock trades its biggest volume in months. That confirms the uptrend will keep going.
questions.why: False. Late in a long run, the loudest day can be the last one. That burst can be the final rush of buyers before the trend runs out. Relative volume of 4.0 or more, especially when the stock's already overbought, can come right before a reversal. Early in a move, rising volume is good. After a long run, it's a warning. That's a day to sell some into the strength, not to buy more.
questions.lesson_line: After a long run, the loudest day can be the last one. Sell some into it.
questions.simple: False. After a long run, a huge volume day can be the last burst of buying before the trend ends.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the loudest day as the strongest proof. Schwab notes high volume can signal the end of a trend, the final surge before it is exhausted. Investopedia's blow-off top is a steep rise in price and volume, followed by a steep, rapid drop.

questions.q: A buddy says his stock went parabolic. What's the price doing?
questions.why: Rising faster and faster. The climb keeps getting steeper, so any trend line under it has to be redrawn steeper and steeper. It's great to own. But these moves can end hard, with a near-vertical top and then a steep, fast drop. If you own one, sell some into the strength and trail the rest under the rising averages. Don't start chasing it up there.
questions.lesson_line: Parabolic moves speed up as they go. Sell some into it, and don't chase it.

wrong.Drifting sideways on low volume: That's a quiet range, the opposite of parabolic.
wrong.Falling in a steady channel: That's a downtrend between two parallel lines.
wrong.Gapping down at the open: A gap down is a one-day jump lower. Parabolic is a run higher that keeps speeding up.

questions.simple: It's rising faster and faster, so the climb keeps getting steeper.

deeper.example: Schwab describes parabolic as a rapid, accelerating rise in price. On a Fidelity webinar the trend line under such a move has to be redrawn steeper and steeper. Investopedia's blow-off top shows how it can end: a near-vertical climb, then a steep, rapid drop.

questions.q: You hear a stock is building a base. What does that look like on the chart?
choices: A one-day gap up on heavy volume
A steady climb with no pauses
The lowest point on the chart
questions.why: A sideways range that lasts weeks. The stock stops trending and goes flat, touching the same areas again and again. It's resting. That's what I want to see after a run. The stock digests the move and the sellers get used up. A base is where the next move starts from. So mark the top of the range and put the name on your radar.
questions.lesson_line: A base is a stock resting. Learn to spot the flat stretch before the next move.

wrong.A one-day gap up on heavy volume: A gap is a single jump. A base takes weeks to build.
wrong.A steady climb with no pauses: That's a trend. A base is the pause.
wrong.The lowest point on the chart: That's one price, not a stretch of time. A base is a flat range that lasts weeks.

questions.simple: A flat stretch where price moves sideways for weeks with no clear trend.

deeper.example: ChartSchool describes basing as a flat trading range without any noticeable trend. Bulkowski's flat base is a price area the stock touches again and again over several weeks or months.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Big investors buying shares quietly while the price moves sideways is called ___.
questions.why: Accumulation. ChartSchool defines it as buying shares without making the price rise much. Schwab explains why: big investors want large positions but cannot buy all at once without pushing the price up. So the chart can look flat and dull while shares change hands. After a decline, ChartSchool says, a stock may base and trade sideways for a long time.
questions.lesson_line: A dull, flat chart can hide big buyers. That's why I keep watching quiet bases.
questions.simple: Accumulation, because big buyers spread out their buying so the price stays flat while they collect shares.

questions.q: You read that a stock is under distribution. What's going on?
choices: Selling that barely moves the price
Buying that barely lifts the price
A company paying out a cash dividend
A one-day crash on panic selling
questions.answer: Selling that barely moves the price
questions.why: Selling that barely moves the price. Big holders are getting out steadily, without dumping it all at once. On the chart you see volume rising while price makes no progress. Here the word has nothing to do with dividends. It's not a crash either, because price barely moves while the shares change hands. When I see heavy volume and no progress, I get careful with that name.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume with no price progress is a warning. Someone may be selling quietly.

wrong.A company paying out a cash dividend: That's the business use of the word. On a chart, distribution means quiet selling.
wrong.Buying that barely lifts the price: That's the opposite, quiet buying. Distribution is quiet selling.
wrong.A one-day crash on panic selling: A crash is fast and loud. Distribution is selling that barely moves the price.

questions.simple: Steady selling that barely moves the price, even while a lot of shares trade.

deeper.example: ChartSchool defines distribution as the systematic selling of a security without significantly affecting the price. Schwab says one hallmark is an increase in volume without an increase in price.

questions.q: When we say a stock is getting tight, we mean its daily swings are small.
questions.why: True. Tight means small candles in a narrow range. The stock's quiet. Quiet stretches are often followed by big moves, which is why tight action gets my attention. And when a strong stock gets tight, your stop can sit close, so the risk is small. That's the kind of spot I want to get involved in.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is quiet. Quiet stretches are often followed by bigger moves, and the risk is small.
questions.simple: True. Tight means the stock trades in a narrow range with small swings.

deeper.example: Investopedia describes a sideways market as prices staying within a tight range. Schwab notes quiet markets make smaller bars. John Bollinger, quoted by ChartSchool, says low-volatility periods are often followed by high-volatility ones.

questions.story: For three weeks a stock's swings keep shrinking: lower highs, higher lows. Volume dries up. It's coiled in the middle of its range.
questions.q: What's the coil telling you about the next move?
choices: A move may come, direction unknown
It most likely breaks out upward
It will break down through the low
It will stay quiet for months
questions.answer: A move may come, direction unknown
questions.why: A move may be coming, but the coil doesn't pick a side. Lower highs and higher lows squeeze the range, and volume dries up. That's the quiet before the storm. Quiet stretches are often followed by big moves. But narrowing doesn't tell you the direction. You find out on the break. So set an alert at the top of the coil and one at the bottom, and let price choose.
questions.lesson_line: A coil tells you to get ready, not which side to pick. Let the break choose.

wrong.It will break down through the low: That's a guess the other way. You only know the direction once it breaks.
wrong.It will stay quiet for months: Quiet stretches are often followed by big moves. That's why you watch a coil.
wrong.It most likely breaks out upward: The story gives no trend for the coil to continue. You only know the direction after the break.

questions.simple: A move may be coming, but the coil doesn't tell you which way. Let the break decide.

deeper.trap: The trap is guessing the side early. ChartSchool calls the narrowing pattern a coil, notes it usually forms as a continuation pattern, and still says the direction can only be determined after the break. John Bollinger notes low volatility is often followed by high volatility.

reasons: only ChartSchool uses the word coil (see conflicts)

questions.q: Your scanner flags a stock at a new 52-week high. What is that high?
choices: Its highest price in the past year
Its highest price since it listed
Its average price over the past year
Its highest close of the past week
questions.answer: Its highest price in the past year
questions.why: Its highest price in the past year, since 52 weeks is a year. It's not the all-time high. A stock can make a 52-week high and still sit under peaks from years ago. A new 52-week high means buyers are paying more than at any point all year. That's strength. Pull up the longer chart too, so you know what's sitting overhead.
questions.lesson_line: A new 52-week high means buyers are paying more than at any time all year. That's strength.

wrong.Its highest price since it listed: That's the all-time high. A 52-week high only looks back one year.
wrong.Its average price over the past year: That's an average, not a high. The 52-week high is the single highest price in that year.
wrong.Its highest close of the past week: A week is far too short. The lookback is 52 weeks, a full year.

questions.simple: It's the highest price the stock reached in the past 52 weeks, which is one year.

deeper.example: Investopedia: a 52-week high is simply the highest price seen over the last year. ChartSchool's new highs count uses the same 52-week lookback, and it reads new highs as buyers willing to pay even higher prices.

questions.story: QRVL just closed at a new 52-week high. WQZN trades 30% below its 52-week high after a long slide.
questions.q: Which one has fewer trapped buyers overhead?
questions.why: QRVL. At a new 52-week high, almost nobody who bought in the past year is holding a loss. There's nobody above waiting to sell just to get even. WQZN sits 30% under its high, so a whole year of buyers is stacked above it. Every rally runs into people who want out. That's why I'd rather buy strength near the highs than a cheap stock after a slide.
questions.lesson_line: At a new high, nobody from the past year is underwater. Far below the high, a trapped crowd waits.

wrong.They face the same: WQZN has a year of trapped buyers above it. QRVL has almost none from the past year.
wrong.WQZN, after its slide: Cheaper isn't lighter. Every buyer between its price and its high is a seller on the way back up.
wrong.Neither, losers just hold: Trapped buyers do sell. Many take the chance to get out near their cost.

questions.simple: QRVL. At a new 52-week high, almost no buyer from the past year is sitting on a loss.

deeper.counter: A new 52-week high clears overhead supply only from buyers inside that window. A stock can sit at a 52-week high and still trade below a peak from years ago, where older buyers wait. ChartSchool explains trapped buyers often sell near breakeven when price returns.

questions.q: Your stock topped at $80 and now trades at $68. How far is it off the high?
questions.why: 15%. Take the drop, then divide by the high. $80 minus $68 is $12. $12 divided by $80 is 15%. Always divide by the high, not today's price. Divide by $68 and you get 17.6%, which makes it look further off than it is. We read every chart this way, in percent off the high, so a $20 stock and a $500 stock compare fairly.
questions.lesson_line: We read a chart in percents: off the highs, extended from the averages.
questions.simple: It's 15% off the high. You measure the drop from the $80 high, not from today's price.

deeper.trap: The trap is dividing by the wrong number. Divide the drop by today's $68 and you get a bigger figure than 15%, so the stock looks further from its high than it is. Always divide by the high.

wrong.17.6%: You divided the $12 drop by today's $68, not by the $80 high.
wrong.12.0%: You took the $12 drop as a percent and never divided.
wrong.85.0%: $68 is 85% of the high. That's what's left, not the drop.

questions.q: There's empty space on the daily between yesterday's bar and today's lower one. What makes that a gap down?
choices: Today's high is below yesterday's low
Today's low is above yesterday's high
Today's range is smaller than usual
questions.answer: Today's high is below yesterday's low
questions.why: Today's high is below yesterday's low. The two days' ranges don't overlap at all, so there's a hole on the chart. A lower close isn't a gap. That's just a down day. Gaps matter because they often act as support or resistance later. A gap down leaves a hole above the price, and that hole is where a bounce can stall. Mark it on your chart.
questions.lesson_line: A gap down leaves a hole above the price. Mark it, because rallies often stall there.

wrong.Today's low is above yesterday's high: That's a gap up, the other direction.
wrong.Today closes below yesterday's close: That's just a down day. A gap needs empty space between the two days' ranges.
wrong.Today's range is smaller than usual: That's a narrow day. A gap is about the space between days, not the size of one.

questions.simple: Today's whole range sits below yesterday's low, so the two days don't overlap and leave empty space.

reasons: fixed before; gap has a second sense in V.05 (our Kicker), see conflicts

deeper.example: ChartSchool and Bulkowski both define a down gap as today's high below yesterday's low. Bulkowski notes gaps are useful for showing support or resistance zones.

questions.q: Your stock gaps up out of a base on heavy volume, a breakaway gap. Gaps like that usually fill within a week.
questions.why: False. Breakaway gaps rarely fill fast. In one big study, only 1% of upward breakaway gaps closed within a week. The small gaps inside quiet ranges are the ones that fill, 85% within a week in the same count. So don't sit out a strong breakaway gap waiting for a fill that may never come. If the setup's there, you buy it with a stop that makes sense.
questions.lesson_line: Don't sit out a strong breakaway gap waiting for a fill. It may never come.
questions.simple: False. Only 1% of upward breakaway gaps closed within a week, so don't wait for a fill.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's figures for upward gaps: 85% of area gaps closed within a week, but only 1% of breakaway gaps did. They cover one week, so they say a breakaway gap rarely closes fast, not that it never closes. ChartSchool warns that waiting for breakaway or runaway gaps to fill can devastate a portfolio.

reasons: numbers that can change: Bulkowski's statistics (re-read 2026-11-12, still 85% and 1%)
statement reworded in wave8 to break the lesson's absolute-means-False pattern

questions.q: After a long run, a stock gaps up on huge volume. Within days it reverses and closes the gap. Which gap was it?
questions.why: An exhaustion gap. It came late in a long move, on heavy volume, and then price reversed and closed it within days. That's the last gasp. Buyers piled in one final time and ran out. You often only know for sure once the gap closes. That's why I sell some into big strength late in a run instead of adding to it. If the gap closes, the move is likely done.
questions.lesson_line: A huge gap after a long run can be the last gasp. Sell some into it and watch whether it closes.

wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts a new move as price leaves a base. This one came as the move ended.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form in quiet, trendless stretches, not at the end of a long run.
wrong.Continuation gap: That one forms in the middle of a move and doesn't get closed fast.

questions.simple: An exhaustion gap. It's the last jump at the end of a long move, and it soon closes.

deeper.trap: The trap is calling it early. ChartSchool says an exhaustion gap counts only if prices reverse soon after and close the gap. Bulkowski says it happens at the end of a trend on high volume and usually closes within a week.

questions.story: A stock broke out of a base weeks ago and has climbed almost straight up. Today it gaps up again on heavy volume. For weeks after, it keeps making new highs and never comes back to the gap.
questions.q: Which kind of gap was that?
questions.why: A runaway gap. It came weeks into a straight-up run, and price kept making new highs without ever coming back to fill it. That's a gap in the middle of a move, also called a continuation gap. An exhaustion gap looks the same on day one, late and on heavy volume. The difference is what comes after. Exhaustion gaps get closed fast. This one never did. That's strength, so don't wait for it to fill before you trust the trend.
questions.lesson_line: A gap mid-trend that never fills is strength. Don't wait for it to close before you trust it.

wrong.Exhaustion gap: An exhaustion gap isn't followed by new highs, and it closes fast. This one did the opposite.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap starts the move as price leaves a base. This one came weeks into the run.
wrong.Common gap: Common gaps form in quiet, trendless stretches and close within days.

questions.simple: A runaway gap. It came in the middle of a fast climb, and price kept making new highs.

deeper.trap: On the gap day itself, a runaway gap and an exhaustion gap can look alike. Both come after a long run, often on heavy volume. Bulkowski tells them apart by what follows: exhaustion gaps usually close within a week, while continuation gaps see new highs without closing. ChartSchool also calls it a measuring gap.

questions.story: A stock ran from $10 to $80 in two years. On your chart, the move from $10 to $20 looks the same size as $70 to $80.
questions.q: Which chart setting shows the $10 to $20 move as the bigger one?
questions.why: A log scale. It spaces price by percent. $10 to $20 is a 100% gain, while $70 to $80 is a far smaller one. On an arithmetic scale every dollar takes the same space, so the two moves look equal. Changing the timeframe or the chart type doesn't change how price is spaced. On long charts and big movers I use log, because percent is what your account feels.
questions.lesson_line: On long charts and big movers, use log scale. Percent is what your account feels.

wrong.A shorter timeframe: Zooming in changes the window, not how price is spaced. The scale is the fix.
wrong.An arithmetic scale: That's the scale you're on. Every dollar gets the same space, so $70 to $80 looks as big as $10 to $20.
wrong.A line chart instead: A line chart joins the closes. It changes how price is drawn, not how the price axis is spaced.

questions.simple: A log scale. It spaces moves by percent, and $10 to $20 is a far bigger percent gain.

deeper.example: ChartSchool: a log scale measures price movements in percentage terms, and an advance from 10 to 20 is 100%. On a plain scale, a move from 10 to 80 shows 10 to 20 the same size as 70 to 80.

questions.q: Today your stock's high is $52.40 and its low is $50.10. What's the day's range?
questions.why: $2.30. The high minus the low. $52.40 minus $50.10 is $2.30. On a candle it's the full height, from the top of the wick to the bottom. It's not the change from yesterday's close. The range matters for your stop. Our stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, the LOD. So if you bought near the high, you're risking a little more than $2.30 a share.
questions.lesson_line: Range is the day's high minus its low. Know it before you buy, because your stop sits under the low.
questions.simple: It's $2.30, the day's high minus the day's low.

wrong.$102.50: You added the high and the low instead of subtracting.
wrong.$51.25: That's the middle of the day, not the range.
wrong.$23.00: Decimal slip. You moved the point one place.

deeper.example: ChartSchool defines the daily range as the day's high minus the same day's low. Schwab notes the vertical height of a bar shows that range.

questions.q: A stock rallies from $40 to $60, then pulls back to $50. What percent of the rally has it given back?
questions.why: 50%. Divide the drop from the top by the size of the rally: (60 - 50) / (60 - 40) = 50%. Dow Theory's Hamilton estimated that pullbacks retrace 1/3 to 2/3 of the prior move, with 50% being typical. ChartSchool's glossary adds that a retracement of more than 2/3 typically signals a trend reversal. These are rules of thumb from history, not guarantees.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a pullback as a share of the rally. Past two-thirds, ChartSchool says a reversal is more likely.
questions.simple: It gave back 50%, half the rally, because it fell halfway from $60 back toward $40.

wrong.200.0%: Flipped it: divided the rally by the pullback.
wrong.83.3%: Gave the $50 price as a share of the $60 top.
wrong.125.0%: Gave the $50 price over the $40 start.

find.label: Share of the rally given back

questions.q: The S&P 500 peaks at 5,000 and falls to 4,400. Is that a correction yet?
questions.why: Yes, it's a correction. Take the drop, then divide by the peak. 5,000 minus 4,400 is 600. 600 divided by 5,000 is 12%. A drop of 10% or more from the peak is a correction. 20% or more is a bear market. In a market like that I get picky. Our market reading in the app tells you how much to trade, and it's worth checking before every buy.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a drop from the peak. Down 10% or more is a correction.
questions.simple: Yes. It's down 12% from the peak, past the 10% line for a correction.

wrong.No, it's down only 1.2%: Decimal slip. You moved the point one place too far.
wrong.No, it's down only 6.4%: You divided the drop by the two levels added together. Divide by the peak.
wrong.No, a correction needs 20%: 20% is the bear market line. A correction starts at 10% off the peak.

deeper.example: Investopedia calls a decline of 10% or more from the peak a correction. Schwab puts a correction at more than 10% but less than 20%, and a bear market at 20% or greater.

questions.q: The Nasdaq Composite is down 22% from its peak after three months of selling. That's a bear market by the usual definition.
questions.why: True. The usual line for a bear market is a broad index down 20% or more over at least two months. Down 22% over three months clears both. The label matters because breakouts fail more often when the market isn't backing them. So I trade a lot less and protect the account first. Check the market reading in the app before every buy.
questions.lesson_line: A broad index down 20% or more is a bear market. Protect the account first.
questions.simple: True. A broad index down 20% or more over at least two months is a bear market.

reasons: one cited fact only (Tier 1); Investor.gov returned 403 to WebFetch on 2026-11-12 (confirmed by the checker on 2026-11-09)

deeper.example: Investor.gov, the SEC's site for investors, says a bear market generally occurs when a broad market index falls by 20% or more over at least a two-month period, a time of falling prices and pessimistic sentiment.

questions.q: You buy on a signal Monday. By Wednesday price has reversed hard against you. What's that called?
questions.why: A whipsaw. The signal flipped on you in a short time. Choppy markets and twitchy indicators cause a lot of them. You can't avoid every one. That's the cost of trading signals. What you control is the damage. A stop a few cents under the low of the day keeps a whipsaw a small loss. And when you're getting whipsawed again and again, the market's telling you to trade less.
questions.lesson_line: Whipsaws are a cost of trading. A tight stop keeps them small, and a string of them says trade less.

wrong.Accumulation: Accumulation is big buyers quietly building positions in a range.
wrong.Breakaway gap: A breakaway gap is a gap that starts a new move.
wrong.Golden cross: A golden cross is a shorter moving average crossing above a longer one.

questions.simple: A whipsaw. The buy signal reversed against you in a short time.

deeper.example: ChartSchool defines a whipsaw as a buy or sell signal that is reversed in a short time, caused by volatile markets and sensitive indicators. Investopedia says you are whipsawed when price abruptly moves the other way right after you buy.

questions.q: You want to draw an uptrend line on your stock's daily chart. Where does it go?
choices: Draw a flat line at the lows
questions.why: Connect the rising lows. The line runs under the dips and slopes up. Two lows draw it, and a third touch confirms it. The more times it's tested and holds, the more it matters. A line across the rally peaks is the channel line, the top edge. Prices often pull back to the trend line before they move on, so it's a spot to watch for an entry.
questions.lesson_line: Uptrend lines go under the lows. The more clean touches, the more the line matters.

wrong.Connect the rising highs: A line over the rally peaks is the channel line, the upper edge.
wrong.Connect the closing prices: That's a line chart, not a trend line.
wrong.Draw a flat line at the lows: A flat line at the lows marks support. An uptrend line slopes up.

questions.simple: Connect the rising lows. An uptrend line runs under the dips and slopes upward.

deeper.example: ChartSchool: an uptrend line has a positive slope and joins two or more lows. It takes two points to draw it, and the third confirms it. Murphy's rule adds that a line tested more often matters more.

questions.q: Your stock just closed under its uptrend line. That means the uptrend is over.
questions.why: False. A broken trend line is a warning, not a verdict. Check it against the swing lows and the support levels. The uptrend holds until price makes a lower low under the last dip. Trend line breaks throw a lot of false signals. So pay attention and keep your stop where it is. Let price confirm before you call it done.
questions.lesson_line: A broken trend line says pay attention. A lower low says the uptrend is done.
questions.simple: False. A broken trend line is only a warning, and the uptrend holds until price makes a lower low.

deeper.trap: The trap is acting on the line alone. ChartSchool says trend line breaks should serve merely as a warning, to be checked with support and resistance or peak and trough analysis. Investopedia says a break could indicate a reversal, and that many false signals occur.

reasons: sources differ in strength (Murphy: usually signals), see conflicts

questions.q: In its first few days, a reversal can look exactly like a normal pullback.
questions.why: True. For a few sessions you can't tell them apart. Both start as down days in a stock that was going up. Only later price action sorts it out. That's why the stop goes in first, before you find out. If it's a pullback, your stop never gets touched. If it's a reversal, your stop takes you out small. Either way you don't have to guess.
questions.lesson_line: You won't know at the start. That's why our stop goes in first.
questions.simple: True. At the start, a reversal and a pullback move the same way, so you can't tell them apart.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the first down days as proof either way. Investopedia says a pullback and a reversal look identical for a few critical sessions. Dow Theory warns that people often mistake a counter-move for a new trend.

questions.q: Everyone's waiting for a pullback to buy your stock. What are they waiting for?
choices: A short dip inside an uptrend
A change from uptrend to downtrend
A break above the last high
A slow sideways drift in price
questions.answer: A short dip inside an uptrend
questions.why: A short dip inside an uptrend. Price backs off for a few days, then the uptrend picks up again. Pullbacks often come back to the trend line or a rising average like the 50-day. That's one of the two classic places to buy a strong stock. A push to a new high is the other. If the dip turns into a lasting change of direction, that's a reversal, and your stop tells you which one you got.
questions.lesson_line: Pullbacks in strong uptrends are one of the two classic places to buy. A new high is the other.

wrong.A change from uptrend to downtrend: That's a reversal. A pullback is temporary, and the uptrend carries on.
wrong.A break above the last high: That's a breakout. A pullback is a dip, not a push higher.
wrong.A slow sideways drift in price: That's a sideways market. A pullback dips lower, then the uptrend resumes.

questions.simple: A short dip in a stock that's still in an uptrend, and then the rise goes on.

reasons: fixed before; pullback has a second, narrower sense in Bulkowski (see conflicts)

deeper.example: Investopedia calls a pullback a temporary dip in an otherwise rising stock price, and in its examples pullbacks moved to near the 50-day moving average before a rebound. It names buying the pullback and buying the new swing high as the two classic entries.

questions.q: A stock rallies into the price where it stalled twice before. Why do traders watch that level?
choices: Selling tends to show up there again
Buyers run out of cash at that price
It is where every stop order sits
questions.answer: Selling tends to show up there again
questions.why: That price is resistance: a price or zone where selling tends to show up and stop a rise. Earlier reaction highs often mark it, like the price where this stock stalled before. Schwab calls it a ceiling. It is not a wall, and a move above it is a breakout. Traders use it to see how much room a buy has before sellers may step in.
questions.lesson_line: Resistance is a ceiling made of sellers.

wrong.Buyers run out of cash at that price: Resistance is about sellers showing up, not buyers running out of money.
wrong.It marks the stock's 52-week low: A 52-week low is a low. Resistance sits at earlier highs that stopped a rise.
wrong.It is where every stop order sits: Stops are placed by each trader. Resistance is a price where selling tends to emerge.

questions.simple: Selling tends to show up at an old high, so that price is called resistance and can stop a rally.

questions.q: Your stock falls through support on heavy volume. How do you read it?
choices: A serious break, sellers mean it
A cue to buy more down here
A sign sellers are running out
A routine move, volume adds nothing
questions.answer: A serious break, sellers mean it
questions.why: A serious break. A drop through support shows a new willingness to sell, and heavy volume says a lot of people mean it. A break on light volume can snap back. On heavy volume it counts for more. If you own it, your stop should already have you out. And we never add to a loser. A stock breaking support isn't a buy just because it's cheaper.
questions.lesson_line: A break of support on heavy volume counts for more. Your stop should already have you out.

wrong.A cue to buy more down here: We never add to a loser. A drop through support shows a new willingness to sell.
wrong.A sign sellers are running out: Heavy volume on a break shows sellers pressing, not tiring.
wrong.A routine move, volume adds nothing: Volume matters here. A breakdown on heavy volume counts for more.

questions.simple: A serious break. Heavy volume through support means a lot of sellers mean it.

deeper.example: Schwab says a breakdown is generally believed to be more significant when volume is high or above average. ChartSchool reads a decline below support as a new willingness to sell.

conflicts: Pullback vs throwback: Bulkowski (glossary, throwbacks page) and Fidelity's Kirkpatrick slides call a return to the breakout price after an UPWARD breakout a 'throwback' and keep 'pullback' for the return after a DOWNWARD breakout. Investopedia, ChartSchool's moving-average page and everyday usage call any short dip inside an uptrend a pullback. The unit uses the everyday meaning for pullback (q63, q39) and teaches throwback only in Bulkowski's sense (q17); no question asks which side of a breakout a 'pullback' follows.

Exhaustion gap: ChartSchool (glossary G and the gaps article) and Bulkowski agree it is a gap IN the direction of a long move, near its end, closed soon. Investopedia's gap page describes it as 'a break lower in prices (usually on a daily chart) that occurs after a rapid rise'. q52 keys the ChartSchool/Bulkowski version; Investopedia's wording is not used.

What counts as a gap: ChartSchool and Bulkowski define it by the whole range (today's high below yesterday's low for a down gap). Investopedia also counts a 'partial gap' (an open beyond the prior close but inside the prior range) and defines a 'full gap' by the open. q50 uses the full-range definition from the two that agree.

Correction: ChartSchool's glossary (C) defines a correction technically, as a decline that retraces 1/3 to 2/3 of an advance. Schwab and Investopedia use the index convention: a decline of more than 10% from a peak (Schwab adds 'but less than 20%'; Investopedia gives no upper bound). q57 asks only for the computed percent and words the 10% line as the convention 'most people use'.

Leader: ChartSchool's glossary defines a leader as an industry or company outperforming the market, and an Interactive Brokers webinar by Dan Russo, CMT, says relative strength shows whether a stock 'is leading or lagging its peers'. Investopedia's 'Market Leader' page is the business meaning (largest market share). Nasdaq's leaders-vs-laggards articles and investors.com refused both clients, and Investopedia's CAN SLIM page (read from the Internet Archive) muddles O'Neil's L ('Laggard stocks are preferred ... Use the relative strength index'), so neither was used. q33 keys the chart meaning and names the business meaning in the reveal.

Base: ChartSchool's 'Basing' is a flat trading range after a decline; growth-stock usage (O'Neil, IBD) also calls a consolidation after an advance a base; Bulkowski's flat base is a flat price area touched repeatedly over weeks or months. q42 keys only the shared part: a sideways range lasting weeks or more, with no clear trend. Base anatomy is V.04's job.

Coil: only ChartSchool (symmetrical triangle page) names the narrowing pattern a 'coil'; I found no second Tier 2 publisher using the word. q46's key does not rest on the word: it rests on the point two publishers agree on, that a narrowing range gives no clue to direction (ChartSchool triangle and squeeze pages; Investopedia sideways market: the old trend may continue or a new one start).

52-week high: Investopedia's 52-week page says the figure is 'based on the security's daily closing price'; ChartSchool and Investopedia's breakout page speak of the highest price. Data vendors differ. q47's answer ('its highest price in the past year') holds either way, and no question asks close vs intraday.

Breakout: Investopedia, ChartSchool and Bulkowski count a break below support as a (downside) breakout; most traders call it a breakdown, as Investopedia itself notes ('a downside breakout, often called a breakdown'). q12 keys 'a move through resistance or support' so neither reading is marked wrong; q13 keys breakdown, and its word bank leaves 'breakout' out so the downside reading cannot make a second right answer.

Extended: ChartSchool's glossary measures it from the pivot (buy point); IBD's well-known 5% buy-zone rule was not used because investors.com refuses this tool's crawler. Our own usage (owner: '% extended from MAs') measures it in percent above the moving averages. q25 and q26 are asked as ours (house: true) with ChartSchool's distance-from-moving-average method as the Tier 2 backing.

RSI levels: ChartSchool notes some traders move the levels to 80/20 and short-term traders use other settings. q28 asks only for the traditional level (Wilder's 70/30, stated by ChartSchool, Investopedia and Fidelity).

Relative strength vs RSI: Investopedia's 'Relative Strength' page discusses RSI as a companion tool in the same article, which blurs the two. ChartSchool's Price Relative page (a ratio against a benchmark) and both RSI pages (average gain vs average loss of the stock itself) keep them apart; q31 and q32 follow those.

Inside day is left to V.03 (candle words).

ChartSchool's glossary T says the same as Murphy ('The breaking of a trend line usually signals a trend reversal'); 'usually signals' is still not 'has reversed', and ChartSchool's trend lines page shows a break that did not reverse the trend.
